blocks.body:
In the plane, the dot product of two vectors is $u\cdot v = |u|\,|v|\cos\theta$, and since $|\cos\theta| \le 1$ it never exceeds the product of the lengths. Written in coordinates, $(u_1v_1 + u_2v_2)^2 \le (u_1^2 + u_2^2)(v_1^2 + v_2^2)$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality says the same holds for lists of any length, where there is no picture to lean on.

This page proves Cauchy–Schwarz, derives its most useful competition form (the Engel form, sometimes called Titu's lemma), generalises it to Hölder's inequality, and adds the rearrangement inequality, which compares sums of products when the order of the terms is shuffled.

blocks.title: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
blocks.body:
For real numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$,

$$\Big(\sum a_ib_i\Big)^2 \le \sum a_i^2 \sum b_i^2.$$

Equality holds if and only if the lists are proportional: one of $(a_i)$, $(b_i)$ is a scalar multiple of the other (this includes the case where one list is all zeros).

Put $A = \sum a_i^2$, $B = \sum b_i^2$, $C = \sum a_ib_i$. If $A = 0$ every $a_i$ is $0$ and both sides vanish. Otherwise consider, for real $t$,

$$f(t) = \sum (a_it - b_i)^2 = At^2 - 2Ct + B.$$

As a sum of squares, $f(t) \ge 0$ for every $t$. A quadratic with positive leading coefficient that never goes negative has at most one real root, so its discriminant is not positive: $4C^2 - 4AB \le 0$, which is $C^2 \le AB$.

Equality $C^2 = AB$ means the discriminant is zero, so $f$ has a real root $t_0$. Then every square $(a_it_0 - b_i)^2$ is zero, i.e. $b_i = t_0a_i$ for all $i$. Conversely, proportional lists clearly give equality.
blocks.title: Proof by a quadratic that cannot go negative
An identity behind the inequality
blocks.body:
There is an exact formula for the gap, called Lagrange's identity:

$$\sum a_i^2\sum b_i^2 - \Big(\sum a_ib_i\Big)^2 = \sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(a_ib_j - a_jb_i)^2.$$

To see it, expand the left side: the products $a_i^2b_i^2$ cancel, and what remains is $\sum_{i\ne j}a_i^2b_j^2 - \sum_{i \ne j}a_ib_ia_jb_j$, which regroups pair by pair into the squares on the right. This gives a second proof of Cauchy–Schwarz and makes the equality case transparent: all the $2\times2$ determinants $a_ib_j - a_jb_i$ must vanish. For $n = 2$ the right side is $(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)^2$, the squared area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors, matching $|u|^2|v|^2\sin^2\theta$.

blocks.title: Engel form
blocks.body:
For real numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and positive reals $b_1, \dots, b_n$,

$$\sum \frac{a_i^2}{b_i} \ge \frac{(\sum a_i)^2}{\sum b_i},$$

with equality if and only if $a_1/b_1 = a_2/b_2 = \cdots = a_n/b_n$.

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the lists $a_i/\sqrt{b_i}$ and $\sqrt{b_i}$ (this is where $b_i > 0$ is used):

$$\Big(\sum a_i\Big)^2 = \Big(\sum \frac{a_i}{\sqrt{b_i}}\cdot\sqrt{b_i}\Big)^2 \le \sum\frac{a_i^2}{b_i}\cdot\sum b_i.$$

Divide by $\sum b_i > 0$. Equality requires $a_i/\sqrt{b_i} = t\sqrt{b_i}$ for a common $t$, i.e. $a_i/b_i = t$ for all $i$.

blocks.title: When to reach for the Engel form
blocks.body:
The Engel form is built for sums of fractions. Its typical use: a sum $\sum x_i/y_i$ can be rewritten as $\sum x_i^2/(x_iy_i)$ (when all $x_i, y_i > 0$), so that the numerators are squares and the inequality collapses the whole sum into one fraction. The art is in choosing the numerators so that $\sum a_i$ is something you know, and the equality condition (all ratios $a_i/b_i$ equal) tells you whether the bound can be sharp.

A quick illustration: for positive $x, y$, $\tfrac1x + \tfrac1y = \tfrac{1^2}{x} + \tfrac{1^2}{y} \ge \tfrac{(1+1)^2}{x+y} = \tfrac{4}{x+y}$.

blocks.title: Hölder's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $p, q > 1$ with $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$, and let $a_i, b_i \ge 0$. Then

$$\sum a_ib_i \le \Big(\sum a_i^p\Big)^{1/p}\Big(\sum b_i^q\Big)^{1/q}.$$

The case $p = q = 2$ is Cauchy–Schwarz (for numbers of any sign, apply it to $|a_i|$ and $|b_i|$). A three-list version often used in competitions: for $x_i, y_i, z_i \ge 0$,

$$\Big(\sum x_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum y_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum z_i^3\Big) \ge \Big(\sum x_iy_iz_i\Big)^3.$$

First Young's inequality: for $x, y \ge 0$, weighted [[amgm|AM–GM]] applied to $x^p$ and $y^q$ with weights $\tfrac1p$ and $\tfrac1q$ gives

$$\frac{x^p}{p} + \frac{y^q}{q} \ge (x^p)^{1/p}(y^q)^{1/q} = xy.$$

Now let $X = (\sum a_i^p)^{1/p}$ and $Y = (\sum b_i^q)^{1/q}$. If $X = 0$ or $Y = 0$ one list is all zeros and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise apply Young to $x = a_i/X$ and $y = b_i/Y$ and add over $i$:

$$\frac{\sum a_ib_i}{XY} \le \frac1p\cdot\frac{\sum a_i^p}{X^p} + \frac1q\cdot\frac{\sum b_i^q}{Y^q} = \frac1p + \frac1q = 1.$$

The three-list version is proved the same way, using $xyz \le \tfrac13(x^3 + y^3 + z^3)$ (AM–GM) after dividing each list by the cube root of its sum of cubes.
blocks.title: Proof via weighted AM–GM
Rearrangement: ordering is everything
blocks.body: Suppose you are paid $a_i$ euros per item for items of $n$ kinds, and you may decide which kind gets which quantity from a fixed list $b_1, \dots, b_n$. Common sense says: put the largest quantity on the best-paid item, the next largest on the next, and so on. The rearrangement inequality confirms it, and also says the opposite pairing is the worst.

blocks.title: Rearrangement inequality
blocks.body:
Let $a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdots \le a_n$ and $b_1 \le b_2 \le \cdots \le b_n$ be real numbers, and let $\sigma$ be any permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Then

$$a_1b_n + a_2b_{n-1} + \cdots + a_nb_1 \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_{\sigma(i)} \;\le\; a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + \cdots + a_nb_n.$$

So similarly ordered pairing gives the largest sum and oppositely ordered pairing the smallest.

Write $c_i = b_{\sigma(i)}$, an arrangement of the $b$'s. If the list $c$ is not in increasing order, there is a position $i$ with $c_i > c_{i+1}$. Swap these two entries. The sum changes by

$$\big(a_ic_{i+1} + a_{i+1}c_i\big) - \big(a_ic_i + a_{i+1}c_{i+1}\big) = (a_{i+1} - a_i)(c_i - c_{i+1}) \ge 0,$$

so it does not decrease. Each swap reduces by one the number of pairs $j < k$ with $c_j > c_k$, so after finitely many swaps $c$ is in increasing order, i.e. $c = (b_1, \dots, b_n)$, and the sum has become $\sum a_ib_i$. This proves the upper bound.

For the lower bound apply the upper bound to $a$ and the increasing list $-b_n \le -b_{n-1} \le \cdots \le -b_1$, then multiply by $-1$.

Positive reals $x, y, z$ satisfy $x + y + z = 1$. Find the minimum of
$$\frac1x + \frac4y + \frac9z.$$
blocks.solution:
Write the numerators as squares, $1 = 1^2$, $4 = 2^2$, $9 = 3^2$, and apply the Engel form:

$$\frac{1^2}{x} + \frac{2^2}{y} + \frac{3^2}{z} \ge \frac{(1+2+3)^2}{x+y+z} = 36.$$

Equality requires $\tfrac1x = \tfrac2y = \tfrac3z$, i.e. $x : y : z = 1 : 2 : 3$, and with the constraint $x = \tfrac16$, $y = \tfrac13$, $z = \tfrac12$. Then the expression is $6 + 12 + 18 = 36$, so the minimum is $36$.
blocks.title: Engel form with a linear constraint

blocks.body:
Prove that for positive reals $a, b, c$,
$$\frac{a}{b+c} + \frac{b}{c+a} + \frac{c}{a+b} \ge \frac32.$$
blocks.solution:
Make the numerators squares by multiplying top and bottom by $a$, $b$, $c$, then use the Engel form:

$$\sum\frac{a^2}{a(b+c)} \ge \frac{(a+b+c)^2}{a(b+c) + b(c+a) + c(a+b)} = \frac{(a+b+c)^2}{2(ab+bc+ca)}.$$

It remains to show $(a+b+c)^2 \ge 3(ab+bc+ca)$. Expanding, this is $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge ab + bc + ca$, which is $\tfrac12\big((a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2\big) \ge 0$. Hence the sum is at least $\tfrac{3(ab+bc+ca)}{2(ab+bc+ca)} = \tfrac32$, with equality when $a = b = c$.
blocks.title: Nesbitt's inequality

blocks.body:
(a) Let $a_1 \le \cdots \le a_n$ and $b_1 \le \cdots \le b_n$. Prove
$$n\sum a_ib_i \ge \Big(\sum a_i\Big)\Big(\sum b_i\Big).$$
(b) Deduce that $(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2) \le 3(a^3+b^3+c^3)$ for $a, b, c \ge 0$.
blocks.solution:
(a) For each shift $k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1$, the pairing $a_i \leftrightarrow b_{i+k}$ (indices taken cyclically, so $b_{n+1} = b_1$ and so on) is one arrangement of the $b$'s. By rearrangement each is at most the sorted pairing:

$$\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_{i+k} \le \sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i \qquad (k = 0, \dots, n-1).$$

Add these $n$ inequalities. On the left every product $a_ib_j$ appears exactly once, so the left side totals $(\sum a_i)(\sum b_j)$; the right side totals $n\sum a_ib_i$.

(b) For non-negative numbers, the lists $a, b, c$ and $a^2, b^2, c^2$ are ordered the same way (squaring preserves order on $[0,\infty)$). Sort both and apply (a) with $n = 3$: $3(a\cdot a^2 + b\cdot b^2 + c\cdot c^2) \ge (a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2)$.
blocks.title: Chebyshev's sum inequality from rearrangement

blocks.body:
Positive reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$\frac1{a^2} + \frac1{b^2} + \frac1{c^2} \ge 3.$$
blocks.solution:
Apply the three-list Hölder inequality to the lists with cubes $x_i^3 = 1/a_i^2$, $y_i^3 = a_i$, $z_i^3 = a_i$. Then $x_iy_iz_i = (a_i^{-2}\cdot a_i\cdot a_i)^{1/3} = 1$, so

$$\Big(\sum\frac1{a^2}\Big)\Big(\sum a\Big)\Big(\sum a\Big) \ge (1 + 1 + 1)^3 = 27.$$

With $\sum a = 3$ this reads $9\sum \tfrac1{a^2} \ge 27$, which is the claim. Equality needs the three lists to be proportional, which happens at $a = b = c = 1$.

The pattern to remember: Hölder lets you multiply the target sum by suitable sums you already know, chosen so that the product of the terms is constant.
blocks.title: Hölder with three lists

blocks.body:
- The Engel form needs every $b_i > 0$. With $a = (1, 1)$ and $b = (1, -\tfrac12)$ the left side is $1 - 2 = -1$ while the right side is $\tfrac{4}{1/2} = 8$.
- Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz means the lists are proportional, not equal. In the first example the equality point is $x : y : z = 1 : 2 : 3$, not $x = y = z$.
- Hölder's exponents must be conjugate, $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$, and the terms non-negative.
- Rearrangement compares arrangements of the same two lists. It needs both lists sorted in the same direction for the upper bound; for numbers of mixed sign, transformations such as squaring may change the order.

Cauchy–Schwarz is the defining inequality of [[inner-products]]: in any inner-product space $|\langle u, v\rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|$, which is what makes "angle" meaningful in high dimensions. Its integral form $\big(\int fg\big)^2 \le \int f^2\int g^2$ was published by Bunyakovsky (1859) and by Schwarz (1888); Cauchy had stated the finite-sum version in his Cours d'analyse of 1821. In probability it says that a correlation coefficient lies in $[-1, 1]$ ([[random-variables]]). In analytic number theory it is everywhere, for instance in the [[large-sieve]] and in bounds for [[exponential-sums]].

Among olympiad tools it sits next to [[amgm]] (the special case AM $\le$ QM is the Engel form with all $b_i = 1$) and [[convexity]], and it is a standard step in [[symmetric-ineq|symmetric inequalities]] and [[geo-inequalities|geometric inequalities]].

1. Prove that $(a+b+c)\big(\tfrac1a + \tfrac1b + \tfrac1c\big) \ge 9$ for positive $a, b, c$.
2. Real numbers $x, y, z$ satisfy $x + 2y + 3z = 14$. Find the minimum of $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ and where it is attained.
3. Verify Lagrange's identity for $n = 2$ by expanding both sides.
4. Use the rearrangement inequality to prove $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge ab + bc + ca$ for all real $a, b, c$.
